prompt: The unlimited tree scores 1.000 accuracy on its training rows and 0.892 on the test months. What does the gap show?
hint: What did the tree do with each training row?

choices.text: It memorised its training rows, noise and all, and the noise does not come back
choices.why: Yes. Noise learned along with signal, and the noise does not repeat.

choices.text: Accuracy cannot be computed on training rows
choices.why: It can, and the 1.000 is that computation.

choices.text: The test months contain mistakes in the labels that the training months do not
choices.why: Nothing points at the labels; the same tree with brakes does far better on the same months.

choices.text: The tree needs more leaves
choices.why: 3,421 leaves for 38,628 rows is already the problem.

prompt: The tree's test accuracy is 0.892 and the always-*stays* constant's is 0.939. By how many percentage points is the tree worse? One decimal place.
hint: Subtract, then multiply by 100.

prompt: Which of these must be chosen on rows the choice did not see? Choose all that apply.
hint: Anything that is chosen, by `fit` or by a person.

choices.text: Which columns the model reads
choices.why: Yes. Picking columns by their test score is fitting to the test.

choices.text: The threshold for sending a credit
choices.why: Yes. A threshold chosen on the test flatters the test score.

choices.text: The model's parameters
choices.why: Yes; `fit` sets them on the training rows and they are judged elsewhere.

choices.text: Which of two models to keep
choices.why: Yes. The winner of a comparison is partly the luckier.

choices.text: The credit's price of R$ 40
choices.why: That is given by the business, not chosen from rows at all.

prompt: Ana scores her model on the test months, changes one setting because of what she saw, and scores again. What is her test set now?
hint: What is a set that is used for choosing called?

choices.text: Still a test set, as long as she reports only the second score and never mentions the first
choices.why: Hiding the first look does not undo it.

choices.text: A training set
choices.why: Nothing was fitted on it; it has been used to choose.

choices.text: Still the test set, because the model was not refitted on it
choices.why: Fitting is not the only way to learn from a set; deciding is another.

choices.text: A validation set with a misleading name
choices.why: Yes. A fresh test is needed for an honest final score.

prompt: Match each set to its job.
hint: One of them is looked at once.
right_distractors: Filling the gaps in the training rows

prompt: In 5-fold cross-validation, how many times is each training row used to fit a model?
hint: It is scored once.

prompt: Five folds give R$ 1,044, 972, 687, 775 and 641 per thousand rows for the same model. What does that spread measure?
hint: What changed between the five fits?

choices.text: How much the model improved from fold to fold
choices.why: The folds are not in order of anything; each fit starts from scratch.

choices.text: A bug, because the same model must always score the same
choices.why: The same model on different rows scores differently, and that is the information.

choices.text: The luck of which rows fell where
choices.why: Yes. A comparison between models closer than this is a comparison of luck.

choices.text: The difference between the five cities
choices.why: The folds are drawn at random, not by city.

prompt: A colleague fits one model on all the training rows, then loops over the five folds scoring it on each. What is wrong?
hint: Which rows did that model learn from?

choices.text: The folds must be stratified when the loop is written out by hand
choices.why: Stratifying would not fix scoring on rows the model saw.

choices.text: Each fold is scored by a model that had already learned from that very fold
choices.why: Yes. It is the training score again, split five ways.

choices.text: Five folds is too few
choices.why: The number is fine; the fitting is the error.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the model was fitted with a fixed random_state
choices.why: A fixed seed makes a mistake repeatable, not correct.

prompt: What does `StratifiedKFold` hold fixed that `KFold` does not?
hint: Compare the two lines of `leavers_per_fold.py`.

choices.text: Each subscriber's rows in one fold
choices.why: That is `GroupKFold`; `StratifiedGroupKFold` does both.

choices.text: The share of each class in every fold, so the folds differ only in the rows they hold and nothing else
choices.why: Yes: 5.70% or 5.71% in every fold against 5.41% to 5.85%.

choices.text: The number of rows in each fold, which KFold lets vary widely from one fold to the next
choices.why: KFold already makes folds of equal size, to within one row.

choices.text: The order of the rows, so that no fold is shuffled
choices.why: It shuffles when asked, as `folds.py` does.

prompt: You call `cross_val_score(classifier, X, y, cv=5)`. Which folds does scikit-learn use?
hint: A classifier and a whole number.

choices.text: Plain `KFold`, unshuffled
choices.why: That is what it uses for a regressor.

choices.text: `TimeSeriesSplit`
choices.why: It never assumes the rows are in time order.

choices.text: `GroupKFold`
choices.why: It cannot group without being given the groups.

choices.text: `StratifiedKFold`
choices.why: Yes, without being asked. A hand-written loop has to choose it.

prompt: When does stratifying the folds matter most?
hint: Think of fifty positives shared among five folds.

choices.text: When the model is a decision tree
choices.why: The folds are the same whatever is fitted on them.

choices.text: When the positive class has very few rows
choices.why: Yes. With fifty positives, one fold can get five and another fifteen.

choices.text: When the classes are about half and half
choices.why: Random folds then come out balanced on their own.

choices.text: When the data has many columns
choices.why: The number of columns does not change how positives are shared.

prompt: For the monthly question, `GroupKFold` scored about the same as random folds. Why did keeping subscribers whole change so little?
hint: Do a person's months share the answer?

choices.text: Random folds already keep subscribers whole
choices.why: They do not; a person's months fall in different folds.

choices.text: There are too few subscribers
choices.why: 7,583 people is plenty; the reason is the question.

choices.text: GroupKFold is broken for categorical data
choices.why: It only reads the groups, not the features.

choices.text: Each month is a fresh event
choices.why: Yes. Grouping matters when the rows of a family share the answer.

prompt: For *will this subscriber ever cancel?*, the top tenth scored 76.0% split at random and 54.7% with subscribers whole. By how many percentage points did the random split flatter the model? One decimal place.
hint: Subtract.

prompt: In which of these should the folds keep a group together? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask whether the model will ever, in production, score a row whose family it saw.

choices.text: Years of listings for a house, predicting its sale price
choices.why: Yes. The listings of one house are near-copies with one answer.

choices.text: Many trips per driver, predicting whether the driver will quit
choices.why: Yes. The answer belongs to the driver, not the trip.

choices.text: One row per customer, predicting the customer's next purchase
choices.why: With one row per family there is nothing to keep together.

choices.text: Several X-rays per patient, predicting the patient's diagnosis
choices.why: Yes. All of a patient's images share the answer.

prompt: The random split scored R$ 1,007 per thousand rows on the same test months where the time split scored R$ 893. Where does the difference come from?
hint: What did the random split let the model learn from?

choices.text: The random split had more rows
choices.why: Quantity is not the reason; which months is.

choices.text: It saw months from after the price rise
choices.why: Yes. The future leaked in as a world, not as a column.

choices.text: The random split is the honest one and the time split is pessimistic
choices.why: The time split is the situation the model will be in.

choices.text: The time split used a worse model
choices.why: Both used the same model and settings.

prompt: In `walk_forward.py`, the model's value per thousand rows roughly doubles from August to September 2025. Why?
hint: Look at the leavers column.

choices.text: The credit got cheaper in September
choices.why: It is R$ 40 throughout.

choices.text: The model was retrained with better settings
choices.why: Every month uses the same settings.

choices.text: September has more training rows than August
choices.why: About ten percent more, which does not double anything.

choices.text: More people left after the price rise
choices.why: Yes: 5.0% to 7.2% leavers. The world moved, and the score with it.

prompt: Snapshots are monthly, the horizon is three months, and the model is fitted on 1 July. How many of the snapshots before July still have no answer?
hint: April's horizon closes on 30 June.

prompt: `TimeSeriesSplit` takes a ___ argument that leaves rows out between the training and the scoring part.
hint: The section's own word for it.

prompt: Put the four questions of the split checklist in the section's order.
hint: Overlap first, the test set last.
items: Is anything in the scoring rows also in training, directly or through a relative?
Is any training row later than any scoring row?
Was every training label known when the model would have been fitted?
Was the test set used to choose anything?

prompt: A bank scores loan applications. Each customer may apply several times a year, and the model predicts default within twelve months. Which split is right?
hint: Three of the checklist's questions apply.

choices.text: Stratified 5-fold, shuffled
choices.why: It mixes time, splits customers and ignores the twelve-month horizon.

choices.text: By date with no gap, since every loan has a date on it
choices.why: A loan from last month has no twelve-month answer yet.

choices.text: By date, grouped, with a gap
choices.why: Yes. Forward in time, no customer on both sides, and only labels that had closed.

choices.text: Group by customer, folds shuffled
choices.why: That fixes one problem and keeps the leak through time.
